rationale: The source gives the standard increasing, decreasing, strict, and monotone conventions. The item extends the wording from an interval to an arbitrary subset and explicitly relates strict monotonicity to injectivity, so it is a semantic adaptation.

The literature gives existence and the supremum/infimum formulas for one-sided limits of monotone real functions. The item packages both monotonicity directions, relative-domain endpoint conditions, uniqueness, and explicit real bounds.

The source gives the removable, jump/first-kind, and essential/second-kind classification. The item fixes a relative-domain convention and separates removable from jump within first kind, a convention-level adaptation.
The sources state that monotone functions have only jump discontinuities. The item adds its precise interior-point and endpoint conventions and the displayed ordering through f(c).
The source states exactly that the discontinuity set of a monotone real function on an interval is at most countable and gives the same rational-in-each-jump injection.

The jump-functions section constructs a nondecreasing sum of summable step functions with discontinuities at a prescribed countable set. The item extends the presentation to every at-most-countable subset of R and fixes explicit weights and empty/finite cases.
The source states exactly that a continuous injective real function on an interval is strictly monotone.
The university notes state exactly that a strictly monotone function on an interval has a continuous inverse on its image and pair it with the continuous-injection theorem used here.
The source states exactly that the Cantor function is continuous on the unit interval.

The source records that the Cantor function is constant off the null Cantor set while increasing from zero to one. The item reformulates “increase only” without importing derivative or absolute-continuity machinery.

The source gives oscillation on a set and at a point by local suprema/infima. The item uses the equivalent pairwise-difference supremum, extended-real empty-set conventions, relative domains, and bounded-function clauses.
The source states exactly, for f:D→R and x∈D, that continuity at x is equivalent to zero oscillation with the same neighbourhood-relative definition.
The source explains that oscillation superlevel sets are closed and continuity points form a G-delta. The item supplies the relative-domain trace formulation and a fully local closure proof.
The sources state that every real function has an F-sigma discontinuity set and G-delta continuity set. The item spells out the oscillation thresholds and relative-domain trace form.
The sources give exactly the Dirichlet indicator and Thomae denominator functions, including the reduced positive-denominator convention.
The sources state exactly that the Dirichlet function is nowhere continuous and Thomae’s function is continuous precisely at irrational points.

The standard characterization says that the continuity sets of real functions are exactly the G-delta subsets of R. The item realizes the set through decreasing open sets and opposite rational/irrational signs, with explicit empty/full boundary cases.
The sources establish that continuity sets are G-delta and that Q is not G-delta by Baire category. The item is the direct library corollary with the canonical-copy convention.

The Encyclopedia of Mathematics gives the classical pointwise Darboux property. The item merges that form with the equivalent arbitrary-interval/every-subinterval image formulation, so it is a semantic adaptation.
The source gives upper and lower semicontinuity and their limsup/liminf forms. The item fixes strict epsilon inequalities on arbitrary real subdomains and adds equivalent neighbourhood envelopes.
The sources give the closed/open level-set characterizations of semicontinuity. The item packages strict and non-strict relative level sets and the continuity-as-both consequence.
The source states exactly that an upper semicontinuous real function on a nonempty compact space attains its maximum, with the lower/minimum statement obtained dually.

Baire category says a nonempty complete interval cannot be covered by countably many closed sets with empty relative interior. The item writes the equivalent nondegenerate-subinterval conclusion in real-line notation.
The sources define Baire class one as pointwise limits of sequences of continuous functions; the Wikipedia convention, followed by the item, includes continuous functions themselves.

The sources state that a Baire-one function has a dense G-delta continuity set and meager discontinuity set. The item strengthens the presentation with closed oscillation superlevels containing no interval and a relative [a,b] formulation.
The source gives exactly Cauchy’s equation f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y) and names its solutions additive functions.
The source states exactly that every additive map satisfies f(qx)=qf(x) for rational q.
The peer-reviewed source states exactly that an additive real function bounded above on a nondegenerate open interval is linear.

The sources list the standard regularity conditions forcing additive functions to be linear and the dense-graph alternative. The item combines six equivalent conditions, both signs, and the explicit dense-graph conclusion in one theorem.

The source gives existence of a Hamel basis of R over Q under choice and unique finite rational coordinates. The item additionally develops coefficient maps, kernels, fibres, and their algebraic properties.

The source explicitly records that the intermediate value property does not imply continuity and gives the standard sin(1/x) witness. The item adapts that construction to the library's nearest-integer-distance oscillator psi(1/x), so the local refutation is source-adapted rather than verbatim.
The sources state exactly that, assuming choice, Hamel bases produce additive functions not of the form cx.
The sources give Thomae’s values and continuity behaviour; the exact oscillation computation 1/q and the bounded-range clauses are a locally expanded semantic version.
The university exercise gives the same weighted sum of rational step functions, monotone and discontinuous exactly at the rationals.
The literature states the prescribed-countable-discontinuity construction, which immediately makes the at-most-countable Froda bound sharp. The item packages that consequence as a separate example.
The notes treat nth roots through the continuous strictly increasing power map and its inverse. The item records the library’s precise nonnegative domain, endpoints, and inverse identity.
The university notes state that the Cantor set is null and that the Cantor function maps it onto [0,1], exactly the example’s core claim.

The open real-analysis text gives the reduced-denominator Thomae construction. The item takes its reciprocal-denominator companion on the rationals, with a finite value on irrationals, and supplies the everywhere-local-unboundedness and denominator-separation proofs.
The sources state exactly that the Dirichlet indicator is Baire class two and not Baire class one because it is nowhere continuous.

The sources construct discontinuous additive maps by prescribing values on a Hamel basis. The item specializes this to one coordinate and adds exact range, kernel, dense-level-set, and dense-graph consequences.

The sources supply semicontinuity criteria and dense-level-set pathological additive functions. The bounded transform and simultaneous no-extremum/nowhere-semicontinuous package is a semantic composition of those standard ingredients.
The source states the one-sided compactness theorem: upper semicontinuity guarantees a maximum, not a minimum. The item supplies a simple explicit counterexample to the reversed extremum.
The university notes state the interval theorem and give the same two-interval, oppositely oriented continuous-injective counterexample showing the interval hypothesis is essential.
